response.translation: Whoever, then, has been trained in the proper manner in the Hippocratic doctrines has learned that of what is now customarily named by all physicians the imperceptible [206] transpiration, by which bodies transpire, one kind is such as vapour, another like dry air, and another issues forth together with perceptible moistures. Something is missing. This, then, is the passage from Lycus' writings, composed to establish that one heat does not differ in any way from another, a passage which does not wait for refutation from outside but overthrows itself. For what does he actually say? 'Heat, insofar as it is conceived as heat, has no variation in relation to another heat.' If, then, 'insofar as it is conceived as heat' signifies nothing in the statement, let it be removed from it entirely. But if it does signify something, it then clearly indicates that in this respect heat does not differ from heat, but that it does differ in some other respect.

For if it differs in no way, the 'insofar as' has been added superfluously; but if it differs in some other way, yet does not differ in this way, then let the differences [207] be conceived according to that in respect of which it differs. So that if indeed one were to consider each thing only according to what it is called, you will abolish the differences of all things. The animal, insofar as it is conceived as animal, differs in no way from another animal. The plant, insofar as it is conceived as plant, differs in no way from another plant. The tree, insofar as it is conceived as tree, differs in no way from another tree. Are there not, then, differences of animal: the winged and the footed and the swimming, and the aquatic and the terrestrial and the aerial, or the mortal and the immortal, or the rational and the irrational, or the tame and the wild, or the cowardly and the valiant, or each of the others that we know? For why need one speak at length? So too among plants, one is a tree, another a shrub, another a thorn-plant, another a herb, another an undershrub. Or, although all things, insofar as they are conceived as animals, have no difference, may one nevertheless not truly call all these that have been mentioned, and besides these not a few others, differences of animal? And so likewise in the case of plants.
uncertain_greek: ἢ τῶν πάντων, καθ’ ὃ νενόηται ζῶα

response.translation: For plant does not differ from plant by one of them being rational [208] and the other irrational, nor by being winged or footed, nor does any of the other differences mentioned apply. Just as animal does not differ from animal by one being a shrub, another a thorn-plant, another a tree, another a herb, another an undershrub, another a cedar; rather, such a division lies within the genus of plants. But Lycus himself also writes of very many differences of diseases, although disease does not differ at all from disease insofar as it is disease, just as symptom does not differ from symptom insofar as it is symptom; yet nevertheless Lycus undertakes to write the differences of these too, as indeed also those of pleuritis and of each of the other diseases. And yet pleuritis does not differ at all from pleuritis insofar as it is pleuritis; but nevertheless one has its pain terminating at the collarbone, another at the hypochondrium. So too one of the pleuritides is accompanied by coloured sputum, while another, contrary to this, is called by some 'non-expectorating', and there are many other differences, in accordance with which it happens that the treatment too is varied.

But Lycus even attempts [209] to teach in detail these differences of the fevers themselves. And yet, whether their generation comes about by an excess of heat or by the biting character of the quality, there will be no difference of fever from fever insofar as it is fever. So uneducated, then, is the argument Lycus puts forward that he does not perceive that he is abolishing all the arts. For the arts are constituted in the knowledge of the differences of each of the things that are. And Plato set this out at very great length in the Philebus, right at the beginning of the treatise; and Aristotle and Theophrastus, Chrysippus and Mnesitheus preserved his view, and there is no one who did not set out the same argument in his writing on art. The first passage of Plato, spoken concerning the constitution found in the arts, is as follows. Socrates: Sound, which passes through the mouth, is for us one, I suppose, and again unlimited in multitude, both for all and for each. Protarchus: Certainly. Socrates:

And we are not yet wise by either of these, neither by knowing its unlimitedness nor by knowing its oneness; but knowing how many [210] they are and of what kind, this is what makes each of us literate? Protarchus: Most true. Socrates: And moreover what happens to make one musical, this is the same. Protarchus: How so? Socrates: Sound, I suppose, with respect to that art also, is one in it. Protarchus: Of course. Socrates: And let us posit two, low and high, and a third, the equal-pitched; or how? Protarchus: So. Socrates: But you would not yet be wise in music knowing only these, while not knowing them you will be, so to speak, worth nothing in these matters. Protarchus: No indeed. Socrates:

But, my friend, when you grasp the intervals, how many they are in number, of sound with respect to highness and lowness, and of what kind they are, and the boundaries of the intervals, and the systems that have arisen from them, which those before us discerned and handed down to us, their followers, to call harmoniai; and again other such affections arising, inherent in the movements of the body, which, measured through numbers, he says must be named rhythms and [211] metres, and at the same time one must bear in mind that thus one ought to examine concerning every one and many. For when you have grasped these things in this way, then you have become wise; and when, examining in this way, you grasp any other of the things that are, you have thus become intelligent about it. These things, then, heard from Plato, would have sufficed for listeners who have sense as a demonstration of the constitution of all the arts. For it is not possible to become skilled in an art even about one thing without knowing their differences. But it is no worse, just as Plato himself was not content with the summary statement alone but added examples for the sake of clarity, grammar and music, that we too should add one further example: of the art of painting, and of the colours, the material underlying it. For it is surely possible here too to say that colour does not differ at all from colour insofar as it is colour, and on this ground to abolish all the differences among them, which indeed Plato himself made clear at the beginning of the Philebus.

For when Socrates was dividing the pleasures, his interlocutor would not concede that they all differ from one another [212] insofar as they are pleasures, asserting that they are most alike; but Socrates meets this argument: 'For colour too, my good man, will not differ at all from colour in this very respect, in being, all of it, colour; yet we all know that black, besides being different from white, also happens to be most contrary to it. And so too figure with figure: in the same way, in genus it is all one, but its parts in relation to its parts are some most contrary to one another, while others happen to have, I suppose, a countless diversity. And we shall find many other things that are so, so that you must not trust this argument which makes all the most contrary things one.' This, then, is the passage concerning colours and figures.

And the one concerning pleasures is this: 'We say that the licentious man feels pleasure, and that the temperate man also feels pleasure in his very temperance; and again that the foolish man, full of foolish opinions and hopes, feels pleasure, and [213] again that the wise man feels pleasure in his very wisdom; and how could anyone who said that each of these pleasures is like the other not justly appear foolish?' Just as Plato indicated the differences of pleasures briefly in this passage, but set them out at greater length through the whole book, so he did those of the arts in two books, the Sophist and the Statesman. Are there, then, many differences of sciences and of pleasures, and of colours and figures and of the tones in voices, and likewise of ages and seasons and regions and diseases, and of all other things, while in hot things alone either there are none at all or they are impossible for men to recognise? And yet Lycus' argument abolishes the differences of the hot, of it alone, as he thinks, but in truth together with all the other things, if indeed the force of the argument can be extended to them likewise in turn. For indeed I shall next say the following about moist things themselves too, saying that these also do not differ from one another insofar as they are moist. But the greatest of his errors is this:

that it also abolishes all the arts, [214] which have their constitution in the differences of the species. Plato, then, having first spoken in summary about the constitution of the arts, also went through the argument by means of an example, showing how the art of grammar was constituted once the difference in vocal sounds had been recognised. But Lycus' argument evidently abolishes this art too, and music likewise along with it, and all the others, claiming that what is taken 'insofar as it is conceived', being a certain thing, has one difference in itself. See, then, how his argument will abolish first the art concerned with letters, and after that all the others too: 'It seems to me impossible and impracticable that this vocal sound, for one who considers it insofar as it is conceived (I mean in respect of the utterance itself), should have any variation in relation to another sound, varying by some peculiarity lying in quality in the utterance.'
uncertain_greek: τὸ δέ τι μίαν ἔχειν ἐν αὐτῷ διαφοράν

response.translation: This argument is in every respect the same as the one written by Lycus at the beginning of the passage, and it is carried through by means of all his very own words, with only the single word for heat [215] changed into that for vocal sound; so that if that argument is sound, so is this one; but this one is certainly not sound, so neither is that one, unless perhaps those who hold Lycus' views think that neither is the sound e different from o, nor does o differ from ō. But if we agree that these too are different from one another, and besides these also a and i and u, and all the other letters, these will be four and twenty. And the art that has recognised their difference is grammar, just as music too is an art concerned with highness and lowness in voices; and yet Lycus' argument abolishes these too no less. For sound does not differ at all from sound insofar as it is sound; but nevertheless the note of the mesē is higher by a tone than that of the lichanos of the mesai, and lower by a tone than that of the paramesē. And of these in turn, the note of the lichanos is higher by a tone than that of the parhypatē of the mesai, while that of the paramesē is lower by a semitone than that of the tritē of the diezeugmenai.
